site.title: UK Folklore by County
site.description: County-by-county guides to folklore, legends, creatures, customs, and strange traditions across the United Kingdom.

pages.title: Where Stones, Spirits and Stories Shape Aberdeenshire
pages.summary: Aberdeenshire is one of Scotland’s richest landscapes for folklore, where prehistoric monuments, coastal traditions, fairy beliefs, ghost stories, witchcraft memories and local song culture have grown around a distinctive north-eastern landscape.

pages.title: Why Anglesey Feels So Full of Legends
pages.summary: Anglesey’s folklore is unusually dense because the island gathers several layers of Welsh story in one place: prehistoric tombs with giant legends, early Christian holy wells, medieval tales from the Mabinogion, memories of Druids and Roman conquest, witch stories from Llanddona, and modern walking routes that turn saints’ legends into lived landscape again.

pages.summary: Angus is one of Scotland’s richest folklore landscapes because its stories grow from several layers of memory: Pictish monuments, medieval saints, powerful families, farming traditions, witchcraft beliefs, haunted buildings, and tales attached to hills, stones, and old roads.

pages.title: What mysteries shaped Banffshire's folklore?
pages.summary: Banffshire is a historic Scottish county where folklore grew from a meeting of coast, river valleys, mountains, farming country and old travelling routes. pages.title: The Strange Stories Behind Buteshire's Islands
pages.summary: Buteshire is the historic county centred on the islands of Bute, Arran, and the surrounding island landscapes of the Firth of Clyde. Its folklore is shaped by a meeting point of sea routes, Gaelic tradition, Christian memory, prehistoric monuments, clan history, and island storytelling.

pages.title: Where Welsh Legends Meet the Mountains
pages.summary: Caernarfonshire’s folklore is best understood through landscape: mountains that hold giants, lakes that hide fairy paths, saints’ wells beside pilgrim roads, and castle mounds where Welsh history turns into dragon legend.

pages.title: Where Caithness Folklore Meets the Edge
pages.summary: Caithness folklore is shaped by edges: the Pentland Firth, the North Sea, the open moor, ruined brochs, old cairns, narrow roads and settlements looking towards Orkney as much as towards the rest of Scotland.

pages.title: Ancient Stones

pages.title: Where Fenland Fear Meets Cambridge Ghosts
pages.summary: Cambridgeshire folklore is less about one famous monster than a whole landscape of fenland fears, household charms, witchcraft memories, saintly healing, university ghosts, Plough Monday customs and chalk-hill giants.

pages.summary: Cardiganshire, now usually called Ceredigion, is one of the richest folklore landscapes in west Wales: a county of sea legends, fairy abductions, holy wells, hillforts, haunted roads, healing relics and stories fixed to very specific places.
